questions.question: When an object moves along a straight path but its speed keeps changing, how can we describe its rate of motion?

options.text: By checking how far it goes every second
By using the total time over the average velocity
By using average velocity over the total time

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**By checking how far it goes every second**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• When an object moves along a straight path, and its speed keeps changing, the best way to describe its motion is by determining its **instantaneous speed**. This can be done by **checking how far it travels every second**.
 
• **Instantaneous speed** is the speed of an object at a particular moment in time. It gives us the most accurate understanding of how the object's motion is changing.
 
• By measuring the distance covered in every second, we can calculate the object's **rate of motion** at that specific point in time, which is crucial for understanding non-uniform motion.
 
• Using average velocity or total time over average velocity is useful for calculating overall motion but does not provide insights into changing speeds at individual moments.
 
• Measuring constant velocity is not applicable here, as the problem specifies that the object's speed is changing.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Instantaneous Speed:**

 
 
• It refers to the speed of an object at a specific point in time.
 
• It can be calculated using the formula: **Speed = Distance / Time**, where the time interval is very small (approaching zero).
 
• Example: A car's speedometer shows its instantaneous speed.
 
 
 
• **Average Velocity vs Instantaneous Velocity:**
 
 
• **Average velocity** is calculated over a longer time interval, whereas **instantaneous velocity** is determined at a particular moment.
 
• For non-uniform motion, average velocity provides limited information about motion changes.
 
 
 
• **Constant Velocity:**
 
 
• When an object moves at a consistent speed in a straight line, it is said to have constant velocity.
 
• This scenario does not apply to cases where the object's speed is changing.
 
 
 
• **Applications of Instantaneous Speed:**
 
 
• Useful in analyzing the motion of vehicles in traffic, where speeds change frequently.
 
• Essential in physics experiments to understand non-uniform motion.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Non-Uniform Motion:**

 
 
• An object is in non-uniform motion when its speed or direction changes as it moves.
 
• Example: A ball rolling down a slope accelerates due to gravity, showing non-uniform motion.
 
 
 
• **Key Formula:**
 
 
• For instantaneous speed: **Speed = Lim (Δt → 0) Δs/Δt**, where Δs is the change in distance and Δt is the change in time.
 
 
 
• **Practical Tools:**
 
 
• Devices like speedometers and radar guns are used to measure instantaneous speed.
 
• In physics labs, motion sensors and data loggers help track changing speeds.

questions.question: How is the mass number of an atom calculated?

options.text: Atomic number multiplied by 3 as an estimate
Total protons plus electrons in the atom
Total electrons plus nucleons in the atom
Protons plus neutrons in nucleus of atom

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Protons plus neutrons in nucleus of atom**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **The mass number of an atom** is calculated by summing the number of **protons and neutrons** present in the nucleus of the atom. This is because both protons and neutrons contribute to the atomic mass, whereas electrons have negligible mass.
 
• The **mass number** is denoted by the symbol **A**, and it represents the total number of nucleons (protons + neutrons) in an atom.
 
• **Protons** are positively charged subatomic particles, while **neutrons** are neutral particles. Both reside in the nucleus, and their combined mass determines the mass number of the atom.
 
• The **mass number** is always a whole number, as it represents a count of discrete particles.
 
• **Electrons**, being extremely light in comparison, do not significantly contribute to the atom's mass. Therefore, they are not included in the calculation of the mass number.
 
• For example, in a carbon atom, the nucleus contains 6 protons and 6 neutrons. Thus, the mass number of carbon is **12** (6 protons + 6 neutrons).

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Atomic Number:**

 
 
• The **atomic number**, denoted by **Z**, is the number of protons in the nucleus of an atom.
 
• The atomic number determines the chemical identity of an element and its position in the periodic table.
 
• For example, hydrogen has an atomic number of **1** (1 proton), and oxygen has an atomic number of **8** (8 protons).
 
 
 
• **Isotopes:**
 
 
• Atoms of the same element can have different numbers of neutrons, leading to different **isotopes**.
 
• For example, carbon-12 and carbon-14 are isotopes of carbon. Both have 6 protons, but carbon-12 has 6 neutrons, while carbon-14 has 8 neutrons.
 
• The mass number changes for isotopes due to the variation in the number of neutrons.
 
 
 
• **Relative Atomic Mass:**
 
 
• Since elements exist as mixtures of isotopes, the **relative atomic mass** is calculated as the weighted average of the masses of its isotopes.
 
• For example, the relative atomic mass of chlorine is approximately **35.5**, as it is a mix of chlorine-35 and chlorine-37 isotopes.
 
 
 
• **Electron Contribution to Mass:**
 
 
• Electrons have a mass of approximately **1/1836** of a proton. Hence, their contribution to the overall atomic mass is negligible.
 
• For this reason, electrons are excluded when calculating the mass number of an atom.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Option 1:** "Atomic number multiplied by 3 as an estimate" is incorrect. The atomic number only accounts for protons, and multiplying it by 3 does not provide a valid calculation of the mass number.
 
• **Option 2:** "Total protons plus electrons in the atom" is incorrect. Electrons are not included in the mass number calculation because of their negligible mass.
 
• **Option 3:** "Total electrons plus nucleons in the atom" is incorrect because electrons are not nucleons, and including them in the mass number calculation is inaccurate.
 
• **Option 4:** "Protons plus neutrons in the nucleus of the atom" is correct, as the mass number is the sum of these two subatomic particles.

questions.question: A body undergoes a displacement of 5 m under the action of a constant force of 5 N, in the same direction as the force. How much work will be done under the action of this force?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**25 J**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Work** is defined as the product of the force applied and the displacement in the direction of the force. The formula is given by:

 **Work (W) = Force (F) × Displacement (d) × cos(θ)**, where θ is the angle between the force and displacement.
 
• In this case, the force applied is **5 N**, the displacement is **5 m**, and the force is in the same direction as the displacement. Hence, the angle θ = 0°.
 
• The cosine of 0° is 1. Substituting the values into the formula:

 **W = 5 × 5 × cos(0°)** = **5 × 5 × 1 = 25 J**.
 
• The work done under the action of this force is therefore **25 Joules**.
 
• *Hence, the correct answer is **25 J**__.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Definition of Work:**

 
 
• Work is done when a force is applied to an object, and the object moves in the direction of the applied force.
 
• It is a scalar quantity, meaning it has magnitude but no direction.
 
• The SI unit of work is the **Joule (J)**, where 1 Joule = 1 Newton meter (N·m).
 
 
 
• **Concept of θ (Angle):**
 
 
• The angle θ represents the angle between the direction of the force and the direction of displacement.
 
• When θ = 0°, the force and displacement are in the same direction, and cos(θ) = 1.
 
• If θ = 90°, the force is perpendicular to displacement, and cos(θ) = 0. In such cases, no work is done.
 
 
 
• **Positive and Negative Work:**
 
 
• Work is positive if the force and displacement are in the same direction (e.g., pushing an object forward).
 
• Work is negative if the force and displacement are in opposite directions (e.g., friction opposing motion).
 
 
 
• **Applications of Work:**
 
 
• Work is a fundamental concept in physics, used to calculate energy transfer in various systems.
 
• It is essential in fields like mechanics, engineering, and thermodynamics.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Work-Energy Theorem:**

 
 
• The work done on an object is equal to the change in its kinetic energy.
 
• Mathematically, **W = ΔKE = 1/2 mv²(final) − 1/2 mv²(initial)**.
 
 
 
• **Practical Examples of Work:**
 
 
• In lifting an object, work is done against gravity.
 
• In compressing a spring, work is done to store potential energy.
 
• In moving a car, work is done by the engine to overcome friction and air resistance.

questions.question: A distance–time graph is a curve rather than a straight line. What does this indicate?

options.text: The body is moving with uniform acceleration.
The body is moving with non-uniform speed.
The body is moving with uniform speed.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**The body is moving with non-uniform speed.**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• A **distance–time graph** represents the motion of a body by plotting distance on the y-axis and time on the x-axis.
 
• If the graph is a **curve**, it indicates that the body is moving with **non-uniform speed**. This implies that the distance covered by the body changes irregularly over equal intervals of time.
 
• A straight-line distance–time graph would signify **uniform speed**, where the body covers equal distances in equal intervals of time. However, a curve represents variability in speed.
 
• **Non-uniform motion** occurs when the object accelerates or decelerates, leading to changes in speed at different points during its motion.
 
• **Acceleration** is not necessarily uniform in this case, as the changing slope of the curve signifies irregular changes in speed over time.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Uniform Motion:**

 
 
• An object is said to be in uniform motion if it covers **equal distances in equal intervals of time**. This is represented by a straight-line distance–time graph.
 
• Example: A car moving at a constant speed of 60 km/h on a highway.
 
 
 
• **Non-Uniform Motion:**
 
 
• In non-uniform motion, the object covers **unequal distances in equal intervals of time**. This is represented by a curved distance–time graph.
 
• Example: A cyclist slowing down or speeding up while riding.
 
 
 
• **Acceleration:**
 
 
• Acceleration is the **rate of change of velocity** of a body. It can be uniform or non-uniform.
 
• If the slope of the distance–time graph changes steadily, the body might be undergoing uniform acceleration. If the slope changes irregularly, it indicates non-uniform acceleration.
 
 
 
• **Characteristics of a Distance–Time Graph:**
 
 
• **Horizontal line:** The body is stationary.
 
• **Straight inclined line:** Uniform speed.
 
• **Curved line:** Non-uniform speed or accelerated motion.
 
• **Steeper curve:** Higher speed.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Key Differences Between Uniform and Non-Uniform Motion:**

 
 
• **Uniform Motion:** Constant speed, straight-line graph, no acceleration.
 
• **Non-Uniform Motion:** Varying speed, curved graph, acceleration present.
 
 
 
• **Real-Life Examples:**
 
 
• **Uniform Motion:** A clock's second hand moving at a constant rate.
 
• **Non-Uniform Motion:** A car navigating through city traffic.
 
 
 
• **Graph Interpretation:**
 
 
• The **slope** of a distance–time graph determines speed.
 
• A **steeper slope** indicates higher speed, while a flatter slope shows slower motion.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT correct about nervous tissue?

options.text: Neuron is made up of axon and dendrites
Examples are brain and spinal cord
Cells are called nerve cells or neurons
Nerve cells are very small in length

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Nerve cells are very small in length**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Neuron is made up of axon and dendrites:** This statement is correct. A neuron, the basic unit of nervous tissue, consists of three main parts: the cell body (soma), dendrites (which receive signals), and the axon (which transmits signals to other neurons or muscles).
 
• **Examples are brain and spinal cord:** This statement is correct. Nervous tissue forms the brain, spinal cord, and peripheral nerves, which are essential parts of the central and peripheral nervous systems.
 
• **Cells are called nerve cells or neurons:** This statement is correct. Nervous tissue is composed of nerve cells (neurons) and supporting cells (glial cells). Neurons are specialized for transmitting electrical and chemical signals.
 
• **Nerve cells are very small in length:** This statement is incorrect. Nerve cells can be incredibly long, with some axons measuring up to 1 meter in humans, such as the sciatic nerve, which extends from the spinal cord to the toes. This makes it one of the longest cells in the body.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Structure of Neurons:**

 
 
• **Dendrites:** Short, branching structures that receive signals from other neurons and relay them to the cell body.
 
• **Axon:** A long, slender projection that transmits signals away from the cell body to other neurons or muscles.
 
• **Myelin Sheath:** Many axons are covered by a myelin sheath, which increases the speed of nerve impulse conduction.
 
 
 
• **Types of Neurons:**
 
 
• **Sensory Neurons:** Carry signals from sensory organs to the central nervous system (CNS).
 
• **Motor Neurons:** Transmit signals from the CNS to muscles or glands.
 
• **Interneurons:** Found within the CNS, they connect sensory and motor neurons and are involved in reflexes and complex processes.
 
 
 
• **Function of Nervous Tissue:**
 
 
• Responsible for transmitting and processing information through electrical and chemical signals.
 
• Controls voluntary and involuntary actions of the body.
 
• Coordinates functions such as reflexes, sensory perception, and motor output.
 
 
 
• **Examples of Long Neurons:** The sciatic nerve, which extends from the lower back to the toes, is an example of a long neuron in humans. Its axons can measure over 1 meter in length.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Neuron Longevity:** Unlike most cells in the body, neurons do not undergo cell division after a certain stage of development. They are designed to last a lifetime but are vulnerable to injury and disease.
 
• **Glial Cells:** These are non-neuronal cells in the nervous system that provide support, protection, and nourishment to neurons. Examples include astrocytes, microglia, and oligodendrocytes.
 
• **Synapse:** A synapse is a junction where a neuron communicates with another cell (neuron, muscle, or gland) via chemical messengers called neurotransmitters.
 
• **Diseases Affecting Nervous Tissue:** Conditions like Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, and multiple sclerosis can damage nervous tissue, affecting its function.

questions.question: What is the formula of plaster of paris?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __** CaSO₄ · (1)/(2)H₂O **__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Plaster of Paris** (POP) is chemically known as **calcium sulfate hemihydrate**, represented by the formula CaSO₄ · (1)/(2)H₂O .
 
• It is produced by **heating gypsum** (calcium sulfate dihydrate, CaSO₄ · 2H₂O ) to a temperature of about **373 K (100°C)**. This process removes water molecules and converts gypsum to plaster of Paris.
 
• Plaster of Paris is a **white powder** that, when mixed with water, forms a quick-setting paste which hardens by reabsorbing water.
 
• It is widely used in **construction, sculptures, and molds** due to its quick setting time and lightweight nature.
 
• POP is known for its **non-shrinking and non-cracking properties** when set, making it ideal for intricate designs and repairs.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Gypsum (CaSO₄·2H₂O):**

 
 
• Gypsum is a naturally occurring mineral and the primary material used to produce plaster of Paris.
 
• It contains two water molecules, which are partially removed during the heating process to form POP.
 
 
 
• **Uses of Plaster of Paris:**
 
 
• **Construction:** Used for making decorative elements like false ceilings and wall moldings.
 
• **Medical:** Utilized in orthopedic applications for making casts to immobilize broken bones.
 
• **Art:** POP is popular for creating sculptures and statues due to its fine texture and quick setting properties.
 
• **Repairs:** Used to fill cracks and holes in walls and ceilings.
 
 
 
• **Other Calcium Compounds:**
 
 
• **Calcium sulfate dihydrate ( CaSO₄ · 2H₂O ):** Known as gypsum and serves as the precursor to POP.
 
• **Calcium sulfate anhydrous ( CaSO₄ ):** A dehydrated form of calcium sulfate, used in industrial applications.
 
 
 
• **Important Properties of POP:**
 
 
• POP is lightweight and fire-resistant, making it suitable for interior decoration and insulation.
 
• It sets quickly when mixed with water and forms a smooth surface.
 
• It expands slightly upon setting, which helps in creating a detailed finish without cracks or shrinkage.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Common Misconception:**

 
 
• Plaster of Paris is sometimes mistakenly identified as gypsum ( CaSO₄ · 2H₂O ), but the two are different.
 
• POP is derived from gypsum by removing 1.5 molecules of water, resulting in the formula CaSO₄ · (1)/(2)H₂O .
 
 
 
• **Handling Precautions:**
 
 
• POP should be stored in a moisture-free environment, as it can reabsorb water and harden during storage.
 
• While mixing, proper ratios should be maintained to ensure effective setting and durability.
 
 
 
• **Environmental Impact:**
 
 
• The production of POP involves the use of gypsum, a non-renewable resource, and releases some carbon emissions during heating.
 
• Efforts are being made to use synthetic gypsum, a by-product of industrial processes, to reduce environmental impact.

questions.question: The fuse wire in electric circuits works on the principle of _________.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**heating effect of current**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The fuse wire in electric circuits operates on the **principle of the heating effect of current**. When electric current passes through a conductor, it generates heat due to the resistance offered by the wire.
 
• The fuse is designed to **protect electrical circuits and appliances** from damage caused by excessive current. If the current exceeds a predefined limit, the fuse wire melts due to the heat produced.
 
• The melting of the fuse wire breaks the circuit, thereby **stopping the flow of electricity** and preventing overheating or short-circuiting.
 
• Fuse wires are typically made of **materials with low melting points**, such as tin or lead, to ensure they melt quickly under excessive current conditions.
 
• This mechanism is a critical component in ensuring **safety in electrical systems**, minimizing risks of fire or damage to appliances and infrastructure.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Heating Effect of Current:**

 
 
• The heating effect of current is a phenomenon where **electric energy is converted into heat energy** when a current flows through a conductor.
 
• The amount of heat generated can be calculated using the formula **H = I²Rt**, where **H** is the heat produced, **I** is the current, **R** is the resistance, and **t** is the time duration.
 
• This effect is utilized in various devices like **electric heaters, irons, and incandescent bulbs**, apart from fuse wires.
 
 
 
• **Induction Effect of Current:**
 
 
• This refers to the generation of an **electromotive force (EMF)** in a conductor due to a changing magnetic field around it.
 
• It is the principle behind devices like **transformers, electric generators, and motors**.
 
• Unlike the heating effect, the induction effect does not involve the generation of heat but rather the generation of electrical energy.
 
 
 
• **Chemical Effect of Current:**
 
 
• The chemical effect of current occurs when electricity passes through an electrolyte, causing **chemical reactions**, such as electrolysis.
 
• Applications include processes like **electroplating, electrorefining, and battery operation**.
 
• This principle is not related to the functioning of fuse wires.
 
 
 
• **Magnetic Effect of Current:**
 
 
• This effect refers to the generation of a **magnetic field around a current-carrying conductor**.
 
• It is utilized in devices like **electromagnets, solenoids, and electric bells**.
 
• While this effect is significant in other applications, it is not relevant to the working of fuse wires.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Materials Used in Fuse Wires:**

 
 
• Fuse wires are typically made of **alloys** such as tin-lead or copper alloy due to their low melting points.
 
• These materials ensure that the fuse melts quickly when subjected to excessive current, providing **efficient circuit protection**.
 
 
 
• **Applications of Fuses:**
 
 
• Fuses are widely used in **household electrical systems**, industrial machinery, and automobiles.
 
• They play a crucial role in preventing **electrical accidents** and ensuring the longevity of appliances.
 
 
 
• **Difference Between Fuse and Circuit Breaker:**
 
 
• While both serve the purpose of protecting circuits, a **fuse melts** and needs replacement after operation, whereas a **circuit breaker** can be reset and reused.
 
• Circuit breakers are more advanced and commonly used in modern electrical systems.

questions.question: For a given material, the resistance per unit length is inversely proportional to which of the following?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Conductivity**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Resistance per unit length** is inversely proportional to the **conductivity** of the material. Conductivity is a measure of a material's ability to conduct electric current.
 
• The formula linking resistance and conductivity is **R = ρL/A**, where **ρ** (resistivity) is inversely proportional to conductivity (**σ**), i.e., **σ = 1/ρ**.
 
• When conductivity increases, the material's ability to allow current flow improves, resulting in reduced resistance. Hence, resistance per unit length decreases with higher conductivity.
 
• Cross-sectional area, temperature, and resistivity influence resistance but are not directly related to the inverse proportionality of resistance per unit length to conductivity.
 
• **Hence, the correct answer is Conductivity.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Conductivity:**

 
 
• Conductivity is the reciprocal of resistivity (**σ = 1/ρ**), and it measures how well a material allows the passage of electric current.
 
• Good conductors, such as **copper** and **silver**, have high conductivity and low resistance.
 
• Conductivity is influenced by factors like the material's atomic structure, temperature, and purity.
 
 
 
• **Cross-sectional Area:**
 
 
• Resistance is inversely proportional to the cross-sectional area (**A**) of the conductor, i.e., **R ∝ 1/A**.
 
• Increasing the cross-sectional area reduces resistance as it provides more pathways for current flow.
 
 
 
• **Temperature:**
 
 
• For most conductors, resistance increases with temperature. This is due to increased lattice vibrations, which impede the flow of electrons.
 
• Materials like semiconductors exhibit a decrease in resistance with increasing temperature.
 
 
 
• **Resistivity:**
 
 
• Resistivity (**ρ**) is a material property that indicates how strongly it opposes the flow of electric current.
 
• It is related to resistance by the formula **R = ρL/A**, where **L** is the length and **A** is the cross-sectional area.
 
 
 
• **Applications:**
 
 
• High conductivity materials like **copper** are widely used in electrical wiring and power transmission.
 
• Materials with specific resistivity values are used in applications like heating elements and resistors.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Electrical Conductivity Units:**

 
 
• Conductivity is measured in **siemens per meter (S/m)**.
 
• For metals, typical conductivity values are in the range of **10⁶ to 10⁸ S/m**.
 
 
 
• **Factors Affecting Conductivity:**
 
 
• Material type: Metals generally exhibit higher conductivity than non-metals.
 
• Temperature: In metals, higher temperatures typically decrease conductivity.
 
• Impurities: The presence of impurities reduces conductivity.
 
 
 
• **Key Examples:**
 
 
• **Copper:** High conductivity, used in electrical wiring.
 
• **Silver:** Best conductor but expensive, used in specialized applications.
 
• **Aluminum:** Lightweight and good conductivity, used in power transmission lines.

questions.question: Which of the following is human-made material and will NOT be broken down by the action of bacteria?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Plastic**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Plastic** is a **human-made material** designed to resist natural degradation processes, including bacterial action.
 
• Unlike organic substances like **Butter, Rice, and Bread**, which are biodegradable and can be broken down by bacteria, plastic is **non-biodegradable**.
 
• Plastics are composed of **polymers**, long chains of synthetic molecules derived from petrochemicals, which do not provide the necessary nutrients or conditions for bacteria to thrive and decompose them.
 
• Plastic pollution is a significant environmental concern because it persists in the environment for **hundreds to thousands of years**, contributing to issues like soil, water, and air contamination.
 
• Efforts to address the plastic problem include **recycling, upcycling, and developing biodegradable plastics**, but traditional plastics remain resistant to natural breakdown.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Butter:**

 
 
• Butter is an **organic material** derived from milk and is rich in fats and proteins.
 
• Bacteria can break down butter during processes like **fermentation and spoilage**, converting it into simpler compounds such as fatty acids and glycerol.
 
 
 
• **Rice:**
 
 
• Rice is a **natural plant-based material** composed mostly of starch.
 
• Microorganisms can decompose rice by breaking down the starch into simpler sugars and organic acids, making it **biodegradable**.
 
 
 
• **Bread:**
 
 
• Bread, being made from flour, yeast, and other organic ingredients, is highly susceptible to bacterial and fungal decomposition.
 
• Bacteria and fungi, such as mold, thrive on bread in warm and moist conditions, breaking it down into simpler organic compounds.
 
 
 
• **Plastic Characteristics:**
 
 
• Plastics are categorized into **thermoplastics** (e.g., polyethylene, polypropylene) and **thermosetting plastics** (e.g., polyurethane, epoxy resin).
 
• They are used in various industries such as **packaging, construction, electronics, and healthcare** due to their durability and versatility.
 
• Environmental concerns arise due to their **non-biodegradability**, leading to accumulation in ecosystems.
 
• Innovations such as **bioplastics** aim to create alternatives that can decompose naturally.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Environmental Impact of Plastic:**

 
 
• Plastic waste contributes to problems such as **marine pollution**, wildlife endangerment, and disruption of ecosystems.
 
• Globally, over **300 million tons** of plastic are produced each year, and approximately **8 million tons** end up in the oceans annually.
 
• Microplastics, tiny fragments of plastic, pose risks to marine life and human health as they accumulate in food chains.
 
 
 
• **Biodegradable Alternatives:**
 
 
• Materials like **PLA (Polylactic Acid)** and **PHA (Polyhydroxyalkanoates)** are being developed as biodegradable plastics.
 
• These alternatives decompose under specific conditions, offering a potential solution to plastic pollution.
 
 
 
• **Recycling Initiatives:**
 
 
• Recycling helps reduce plastic waste by converting it into reusable products.
 
• Advanced technologies like **chemical recycling** break down plastic into its original monomers for reuse.
 
 
 
• **Global Policies:**
 
 
• Countries are implementing bans on single-use plastics. For example, **India** banned single-use plastic items such as straws and cutlery in **July 2022**.
 
• International initiatives like the **United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP)** advocate for reducing plastic production and encouraging sustainable alternatives.

questions.question: Arrange the following metals: K, Ca, Al in the order of increasing reactivity.

The correct answer is __**Al [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Reactivity of metals** is determined by their tendency to lose electrons and form positive ions. This is influenced by their position in the periodic table.
 
• In the given metals, **Potassium (K)**, **Calcium (Ca)**, and **Aluminum (Al)**, the reactivity increases as we move down a group or to the left across a period.
 
• **Potassium (K)** is in Group 1 of the periodic table, making it highly reactive. Alkali metals like potassium have low ionization energy and readily lose their single valence electron.
 
• **Calcium (Ca)** belongs to Group 2, the alkaline earth metals. It is less reactive than potassium but more reactive than aluminum because it has two valence electrons that are fairly easy to lose.
 
• **Aluminum (Al)** is in Group 13 and is less reactive than potassium and calcium. Although it has three valence electrons, the effective nuclear charge is higher, making it more difficult for aluminum to lose electrons compared to potassium and calcium.
 
• Therefore, the correct order of increasing reactivity is **Al 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Reactivity Trends in Groups and Periods:**

 
 
• In a group, reactivity increases as we move down because the atomic size increases, and the outermost electrons are farther from the nucleus, making them easier to lose.
 
• In a period, reactivity decreases from left to right because the effective nuclear charge increases, pulling the electrons closer to the nucleus and making them harder to lose.
 
 
 
• **Reactivity of Potassium:**
 
 
• Potassium is a soft, silvery-white metal that reacts violently with water to form potassium hydroxide and hydrogen gas.
 
• It is stored in oil to prevent a reaction with moisture and oxygen in the air.
 
 
 
• **Reactivity of Calcium:**
 
 
• Calcium reacts with water more slowly than potassium to form calcium hydroxide and hydrogen gas.
 
• It is used in construction (lime and cement) and as a reducing agent in the extraction of other metals.
 
 
 
• **Reactivity of Aluminum:**
 
 
• Aluminum is less reactive due to the formation of a protective oxide layer that prevents further reactions.
 
• It is widely used in industries for its lightweight and corrosion-resistant properties.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Activity Series of Metals:** The activity series ranks metals based on their reactivity. Potassium is at the top, followed by calcium, while aluminum is much lower in the series.
 
• **Displacement Reactions:** More reactive metals can displace less reactive metals from their compounds. For example, potassium can displace calcium or aluminum from their respective compounds.
 
• **Practical Applications:**
 
 
• Potassium compounds are used in fertilizers and fireworks due to their high reactivity.
 
• Calcium is used in the metallurgical industry and as a deoxidizer in steel production.
 
• Aluminum is used in packaging, transportation, and construction due to its strength-to-weight ratio and resistance to corrosion.

questions.question: Which of the following defines cross-pollination correctly?

options.text: Transfer of pollen from one plant to a non-flowering plant
Fertilisation of an ovule without pollen transfer
Transfer of pollen from the anther of one flower to the stigma of another flower
Transfer of pollen within the same flower

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Transfer of pollen from the anther of one flower to the stigma of another flower**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Cross-pollination** refers to the transfer of **pollen grains** from the anther of one flower to the stigma of another flower of the same species. This is the correct definition of cross-pollination.
 
• It is a type of sexual reproduction in plants that ensures **genetic diversity**, as pollen from a different plant is introduced to the ovule of another plant.
 
• This process often involves external agents like **wind, water, insects, or animals** to facilitate the transfer of pollen.
 
• Cross-pollination is important for plants to adapt to changing environments and evolve, as it introduces genetic variations in the species.
 
• The other options provided in the question are incorrect as they do not align with the scientific definition of cross-pollination.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Self-Pollination**:

 
 
• Self-pollination occurs when **pollen grains** are transferred from the anther to the stigma of the same flower or another flower on the same plant.
 
• This process requires no external agents and results in **genetically identical offspring** to the parent plant, maintaining genetic uniformity.
 
 
 
• **Agents of Cross-Pollination**:
 
 
• **Wind (Anemophily)**: Plants like maize and wheat rely on wind to carry their lightweight pollen grains to other flowers.
 
• **Insects (Entomophily)**: Insect-pollinated plants like sunflowers and roses produce colorful flowers and nectar to attract bees, butterflies, and other insects.
 
• **Water (Hydrophily)**: Aquatic plants like seagrasses utilize water currents to transfer pollen between flowers.
 
• **Animals (Zoophily)**: Birds, bats, and other animals also aid in cross-pollination by carrying pollen from one flower to another as they feed.
 
 
 
• **Importance of Cross-Pollination**:
 
 
• Ensures **genetic variation**, which is crucial for the survival and evolution of plant species in changing environmental conditions.
 
• Increases the chances of plants adapting to new pests, diseases, and climates, enhancing **ecological resilience**.
 
• Many fruits, vegetables, and grains depend on cross-pollination, making it essential for **agriculture and food production**.
 
 
 
• **Incorrect Options Explained**:
 
 
• **Option 1:** "Transfer of pollen from one plant to a non-flowering plant" is incorrect as non-flowering plants reproduce differently (e.g., through spores).
 
• **Option 2:** "Fertilization of an ovule without pollen transfer" is incorrect as fertilization in plants involves pollen transfer for sexual reproduction.
 
• **Option 4:** "Transfer of pollen within the same flower" refers to **self-pollination**, not cross-pollination.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Cross-Pollination Examples**:

 
 
• Plants like apple, mango, and cucumber depend on cross-pollination for fruit production.
 
• Insects like honeybees play a significant role in pollinating crops such as almonds and blueberries.
 
 
 
• **Impact on Agriculture**:
 
 
• Cross-pollination is vital for high crop yields, ensuring better quality fruits and seeds.
 
• A decline in pollinator populations, such as bees, can negatively impact agricultural productivity.
 
 
 
• **Fun Fact**:
 
 
• The world's most expensive spice, **saffron**, is produced from flowers that rely on manual cross-pollination due to their unique structure.

questions.question: The sexual act is a very intimate connection of bodies and there are many diseases that can be transmitted sexually. Which of the following is caused by bacteria?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Both gonorrhoea and syphilis**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Syphilis:** Syphilis is a sexually transmitted disease caused by the bacterium **Treponema pallidum**. It can lead to serious health complications if left untreated, including damage to the brain, nerves, and other organs.
 
• **Gonorrhoea:** Gonorrhoea is caused by the bacterium **Neisseria gonorrhoeae**. This infection affects mucous membranes of the reproductive tract, as well as the mouth, throat, eyes, and rectum.
 
• Both syphilis and gonorrhoea are bacterial infections, making **antibiotic treatment** effective in managing these diseases if diagnosed early.
 
• These sexually transmitted infections (STIs) are primarily spread through unprotected sexual contact. Practicing safe sex and regular health check-ups are essential for prevention.
 
• **Warts:** Warts are caused by the **human papillomavirus (HPV)**, which is a virus, not a bacterium. This makes them different from bacterial STIs like syphilis and gonorrhoea.
 
• **Key difference:** Syphilis and gonorrhoea are bacterial infections, while warts are viral, highlighting the importance of distinguishing between different types of STIs.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Syphilis:**

 
 
• **Stages:** Syphilis progresses through primary, secondary, latent, and tertiary stages. Each stage has distinct symptoms, from painless sores to neurological damage in advanced stages.
 
• **Detection:** Syphilis can be diagnosed through blood tests, including rapid plasma reagin (RPR) and treponemal antibody tests.
 
• **Treatment:** The standard treatment for syphilis is **penicillin**, which is highly effective in all stages of the infection.
 
• **Global impact:** Syphilis remains a significant public health issue in developing countries. Efforts to control it include early diagnosis and treatment campaigns.
 
 
 
• **Gonorrhoea:**
 
 
• **Symptoms:** Gonorrhoea symptoms include painful urination, discharge, and pelvic pain. However, it can also be asymptomatic, making regular testing crucial.
 
• **Antibiotic resistance:** Gonorrhoea has shown increasing resistance to antibiotics, with **cephalosporins** being the current recommended treatment.
 
• **Prevention:** Using condoms and reducing the number of sexual partners can lower the risk of gonorrhoea transmission.
 
• **Complications:** Untreated gonorrhoea can lead to infertility, pelvic inflammatory disease, and systemic infections.
 
 
 
• **Human Papillomavirus (HPV):**
 
 
• **Cause of warts:** HPV is responsible for genital warts and cervical cancer. It is transmitted through skin-to-skin contact during sexual activity.
 
• **Vaccine:** HPV vaccines like **Gardasil** and Cervarix are effective in preventing high-risk strains of HPV.
 
• **Detection:** HPV is diagnosed via Pap smear tests and HPV DNA tests.
 
• **Global prevalence:** HPV is one of the most common STIs globally, with millions of new cases reported annually.
 
 
 
• **Important Points:**
 
 
• **Education:** Comprehensive sexual education is essential to raise awareness about STIs, their symptoms, prevention, and treatment.
 
• **Regular screening:** Regular STI screenings are crucial, especially for sexually active individuals, to ensure early detection and treatment.
 
• **Public health initiatives:** Governments and health organizations worldwide run campaigns to promote safe sexual practices and reduce the spread of STIs.

questions.question: What is the SI unit of pressure used in measuring gases?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Pascal**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Pascal (Pa)** is the **SI unit of pressure**. It is defined as one newton per square meter (**N/m²**).
 
• Pressure is mathematically expressed as the force applied per unit area: **Pressure = Force / Area**.
 
• In gas measurement, pressure is crucial for understanding the behavior of gases under different conditions, following the principles of gas laws like Boyle's Law and Charles's Law.
 
• The name "Pascal" honors the French mathematician and physicist **Blaise Pascal**, who made significant contributions to fluid mechanics and pressure studies.
 
• Pascal is widely used in various scientific and engineering fields, including meteorology, thermodynamics, and fluid dynamics, to measure gas pressure, atmospheric pressure, and other related quantities.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Kelvin:**

 
 
• Kelvin (**K**) is the SI unit of **temperature**, not pressure.
 
• It is used to measure the absolute temperature of gases, which is crucial for understanding gas behavior under the laws of thermodynamics.
 
• The Kelvin scale starts at absolute zero, the point where all molecular motion theoretically ceases.
 
 
 
• **Newton:**
 
 
• Newton (**N**) is the SI unit of **force**, not pressure.
 
• It is defined as the force required to accelerate a mass of one kilogram by one meter per second squared (**kg·m/s²**).
 
• Newton is used in the calculation of pressure but is not itself a direct measure of pressure.
 
 
 
• **Joule:**
 
 
• Joule (**J**) is the SI unit of **energy**, not pressure.
 
• It is defined as the energy transferred when a force of one newton is applied over a distance of one meter.
 
• Joules are used in thermodynamics to calculate the energy associated with gases but are not relevant to pressure measurement.
 
 
 
• **Applications of Pascal:**
 
 
• Widely used in **engineering, meteorology, and fluid mechanics** to measure quantities like gas pressure, atmospheric pressure, and hydraulic pressure.
 
• One practical example is the measurement of **tire pressure**, which is often expressed in kilopascals (**kPa**).
 
• Atmospheric pressure at sea level is approximately **101,325 Pa**, which is equivalent to **1 atm** (standard atmospheric pressure).
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Gas Laws and Pressure:**

 
 
• **Boyle's Law:** At constant temperature, the pressure of a gas is inversely proportional to its volume (**P ∝ 1/V**).
 
• **Charles's Law:** At constant pressure, the volume of a gas is directly proportional to its absolute temperature (**V ∝ T**).
 
• **Ideal Gas Law:** The relationship between pressure, volume, and temperature is expressed as **PV = nRT**, where **R** is the universal gas constant.
 
 
 
• **Pressure Conversions:**
 
 
• **1 atm** = 101,325 Pa = 760 mmHg = 14.7 psi (pounds per square inch).
 
• These conversions are crucial for applications in different fields, such as aviation, weather forecasting, and industrial processes.

questions.question: What is the transformation of a larva into an adult frog through drastic changes called?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Metamorphosis**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Metamorphosis** is the biological process through which a larva transforms into an adult frog, involving drastic physical and physiological changes.
 
• During metamorphosis, the tadpole undergoes significant changes such as the development of **limbs**, loss of the **tail**, and the formation of **lungs** for breathing air instead of gills.
 
• This process is characteristic of amphibians like frogs and is regulated by hormones, primarily **thyroxine** produced by the thyroid gland.
 
• Metamorphosis occurs in distinct stages: **egg, larva (tadpole), and adult**, marking the frog’s transition from an aquatic to a terrestrial lifestyle.
 
• The changes during metamorphosis enable the adult frog to adapt to new habitats and perform essential functions such as reproduction and survival on land.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Stages of Frog Life Cycle:**

 
 
• **Egg Stage:** Frogs lay eggs in water, which hatch into larvae called tadpoles.
 
• **Larva (Tadpole) Stage:** Tadpoles have tails, gills, and a herbivorous diet. They are entirely aquatic at this stage.
 
• **Adult Stage:** After metamorphosis, adult frogs develop lungs, limbs, and lose their tails, becoming capable of living both in water and on land.
 
 
 
• **Role of Hormones:**
 
 
• The thyroid hormone **thyroxine** is crucial in regulating metamorphosis. Its concentration determines the pace of transformation.
 
• Other hormones like prolactin also play a role in maintaining larval characteristics until metamorphosis begins.
 
 
 
• **Adaptations in Adult Frogs:**
 
 
• Adult frogs have **lungs** for breathing air and **moist skin** for cutaneous respiration.
 
• They develop **strong hind limbs** for jumping and swimming.
 
• Frogs shift to a carnivorous diet, feeding on insects and other small organisms.
 
 
 
• **Other Animals Undergoing Metamorphosis:**
 
 
• Metamorphosis is common in **insects** (e.g., butterflies, moths), **amphibians** (e.g., frogs, toads), and some **marine species** like starfish.
 
• In insects, metamorphosis can be complete (egg, larva, pupa, adult) or incomplete (egg, nymph, adult).
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Metamorphosis vs. Direct Development:**

 
 
• **Metamorphosis:** Involves drastic changes in form and function during the life cycle (e.g., frogs, insects).
 
• **Direct Development:** In some species, there are no drastic changes, and offspring resemble miniature adults (e.g., humans, reptiles).
 
 
 
• **Environmental Influence:**
 
 
• Factors like **temperature**, **water quality**, and availability of **food** can impact the rate and success of metamorphosis.
 
• Pollution and habitat destruction can hinder the normal development of amphibians.
 
 
 
• **Scientific Importance:**
 
 
• Studying metamorphosis helps scientists understand **growth, development, and hormonal regulation** in organisms.
 
• Amphibians are considered **bio-indicators** for ecological health due to their sensitivity to environmental changes.

questions.question: What is mixed cropping?

options.text: Growing multiple crops on a field in the same season
Alternating between growing crops in one season and leaving the field empty in the following season
Growing the same crop on a field in all seasons
Rotating crops on a field seasonally

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Growing multiple crops on a field in the same season**__.
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 

__ 
 
• **Mixed Cropping** is an agricultural practice where **two or more crops are grown simultaneously on the same piece of land** during a single growing season. 
 
• The main objective of mixed cropping is to **maximize resource utilization**, such as sunlight, water, and soil nutrients, while minimizing risks associated with crop failure. 
 
• Different types of crops, such as cereals and legumes, are often grown together to **enhance soil fertility**. For example, wheat and gram, or maize and beans, are common combinations. 
 
• Mixed cropping helps in **pest and disease management** as different crops can repel or resist specific pests and diseases more effectively than a monoculture. 
 
• This method is particularly useful in regions with **unreliable rainfall** or limited irrigation facilities, as it ensures better chances of yield from at least one crop. 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 

__ 
 
• **Benefits of Mixed Cropping:** 
 
 
• **Risk Mitigation:** Mixed cropping reduces the risk of total crop failure, as different crops respond differently to environmental conditions. 
 
• **Improved Soil Health:** Growing legumes alongside cereals improves soil fertility through nitrogen fixation. 
 
• **Increased Biodiversity:** It promotes biodiversity in agricultural fields, which benefits the ecosystem. 
 
• **Efficient Land Use:** Mixed cropping ensures optimal use of available land and resources. 
 
 
 
• **Examples of Mixed Cropping:** 
 
 
• **Wheat + Mustard:** Commonly practiced in North India to utilize different growth patterns and nutrient needs. 
 
• **Sorghum + Pigeon Pea:** Suitable for semi-arid regions. 
 
• **Maize + Cowpea:** A common practice for fodder production. 
 
 
 
• **Difference between Mixed Cropping and Intercropping:** 
 
 
• **Mixed Cropping:** Crops are grown together without any specific arrangement. 
 
• **Intercropping:** Crops are grown in a specific pattern, such as rows or strips, to ensure better management and yield. 
 
 
 
• **Limitations of Mixed Cropping:** 
 
 
• **Competition:** Crops may compete for sunlight, water, and nutrients, potentially reducing yield. 
 
• **Complexity:** It requires careful crop selection and management to ensure compatibility and avoid adverse effects. 
 
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 

 
 
• **Other Cropping Systems:** 
 
 
• **Monocropping:** Growing only one type of crop on a field in a single season. It is simple but risky due to pests and diseases. 
 
• **Crop Rotation:** Rotating different crops in different seasons to improve soil fertility and reduce pest buildup. 
 
• **Relay Cropping:** Planting a second crop before the first crop is harvested, ensuring continuous crop production. 
 
 
 
• **Historical Context:** Mixed cropping has been practiced for centuries in traditional agriculture, especially in subsistence farming systems.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly lists the components of the vascular tissue known as xylem?

options.text: Tracheids, vessels, sieve tubes, xylem parenchyma
Companion cells, sieve cells, vessels, tracheids
Tracheids, vessels, xylem parenchyma, xylem fibres
Sieve tubes, companion cells, phloem fibres, phloem parenchyma

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Tracheids, vessels, xylem parenchyma, xylem fibres**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Xylem** is one of the two types of vascular tissues in plants, the other being phloem. Its primary function is the conduction of water and dissolved minerals from the roots to other parts of the plant.
 
• The main components of xylem include:
 
 
• **Tracheids:** These are elongated, tube-like cells with thickened lignified walls. They are dead cells and lack protoplasm, allowing efficient water conduction.
 
• **Vessels:** These are cylindrical tube-like structures formed from a series of vessel elements. They are also dead and function as the primary water-conducting cells in angiosperms.
 
• **Xylem Parenchyma:** These are the only living cells in xylem. They store food materials and assist in lateral conduction of water.
 
• **Xylem Fibres:** These are sclerenchymatous fibres that provide mechanical support to the plant.
 
 
 
• The combination of tracheids, vessels, xylem parenchyma, and xylem fibres ensures both the conduction of water and minerals and structural support in vascular plants.
 
• **Sieve tubes, companion cells, phloem parenchyma, and phloem fibres** belong to the phloem tissue, not xylem, making options with these components incorrect.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Tracheids:**

 
 
• Found in both gymnosperms and angiosperms, but they are the primary water-conducting cells in gymnosperms.
 
• They have pits for water movement between adjacent cells.
 
 
 
• **Vessels:**
 
 
• They are more efficient in water conduction than tracheids due to their larger diameter and continuous column formation.
 
• Vessels are a characteristic feature of angiosperms.
 
 
 
• **Xylem Parenchyma:**
 
 
• It stores starch, fats, tannins, and other substances.
 
• It assists in the radial conduction of water through the plant body.
 
 
 
• **Xylem Fibres:**
 
 
• Provide structural strength to the plant.
 
• They are highly lignified and non-living.
 
 
 
• **Phloem Tissue:**
 
 
• The phloem is responsible for the transport of organic nutrients, primarily sugars, from leaves to other parts of the plant.
 
• Its components include sieve tubes, companion cells, phloem parenchyma, and phloem fibres.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Function of Xylem:**

 
 
• Xylem conducts water and mineral nutrients from the roots to aerial parts of the plant.
 
• It provides mechanical support to the plant due to its lignified cell walls.
 
 
 
• **Comparison of Xylem and Phloem:**
 
 
• Xylem transports water and minerals, while phloem transports food (sucrose) and other organic materials.
 
• Xylem tissues are mostly dead at maturity, whereas phloem tissues are mostly living.
 
 
 
• **Significance of Water Conduction:**
 
 
• Water is essential for photosynthesis, transpiration, and maintaining cell turgidity.
 
• Xylem plays a critical role in plant survival, especially in tall trees where water needs to be transported to great heights.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of the 'enrichment of ores' process in metallurgy?

options.text: To refine the extracted metal to increase its purity.
To combine the metal with other elements to form alloys.
To remove undesirable impurities (gangue) from the ore.
To convert the metal ore into its molten form.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**To remove undesirable impurities (gangue) from the ore**__.

• The process of **enrichment of ores**, also called ore concentration, is a critical step in metallurgy where the goal is to **remove gangue (unwanted impurities)** such as sand, clay, and rocks from the ore.
 
• Gangue materials are non-metallic and do not contain the valuable metal. Their removal ensures a higher concentration of the desired metal in the ore.
